claims.text: High configurational entropy promotes surface segregation of strong oxide-forming elements such as Al or Cr.
Surface-segregated oxide-forming elements nucleate and grow a dense, adherent, slow-growing oxide film.
The resulting oxide film acts as an oxygen-diffusion barrier.
The initial material is a homogeneous high-entropy alloy containing multiple principal elements and at least one strong oxide-forming element.
The proposed oxidation exposure is in air or an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 800–1200°C for a controlled duration.
Surface enrichment of oxide-forming elements leads to a continuous, dense oxide layer.
High configurational entropy reduces diffusion kinetics at elevated temperature.
Reduced diffusion kinetics promote selective segregation of oxide-forming elements to the surface.
Selective oxidation of the segregated elements forms a stable oxide film.
The stable oxide film impedes oxygen ingress and slows subsequent oxidation.
Relative to lower-entropy conventional alloys with similar oxide-former content, the high-entropy alloy will form a thinner oxide layer.
Relative to the conventional baseline, the high-entropy alloy will form a more continuous and adherent oxide layer.
Relative to the conventional baseline, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit a lower oxidation rate and greater resistance to spallation.
The proposed baseline consists of single-principal-element or low-entropy alloys with similar nominal oxide-former contents.
The hypothesis is limited to high-entropy alloys containing sufficient concentrations of strong oxide-forming elements under oxidizing conditions at 800–1200°C.
Competing phases can interfere with protective oxide growth.
Variations in processing may affect oxide-layer properties.

Increasing oxide-former concentration or surface-enrichment potential should produce a more continuous, adherent, diffusion-resistant oxide with lower mass gain and a slower oxidation rate than the conventional baseline.
